items.title: New Agroclimate App Delivers Real-Time Climate & Crop Insights
items.description: BLACKSBURG, Va. — For years, farmers have had to rely on nothing more than experience and a watchful eye on the sky to make weather-based decisions. Now, with just a few taps, they can access satellite-powered data that helps them decide when to water, fertilize, and harvest — all through a new app from researchers […] The post New Agroclimate App Delivers Real-Time Climate & Crop Insights appeared first on Morning Ag Clips.
items.summary:
The app provides real-time insights into crop health, weather forecasts, soil conditions, and climate patterns to help farmers make more informed decisions.

Key details:
- The app was developed by Abhilash Chandel, assistant professor of precision agriculture technologies at Virginia Tech.
- It is built on Google Earth Engine and uses open-access satellite, weather, and soil data to deliver insights.
- The app can be used for over 45 crop types and is applicable to open-field farming systems worldwide.
- Key data sources include Sentinel-2 satellites, NASA's Soil Moisture Active Passive satellite, NOAA's global forecast system, and the International Soil Reference and Information Centre.
- Data is updated frequently, with weather forecasts refreshed daily and satellite imagery updated every 4 days.
- The app contains tutorial videos and the researchers are conducting demonstrations across Virginia and nationwide.
- Future plans include integration with on-farm equipment and drone data processing, as well as AI and climate modeling advances.
- The project has received funding support from Cotton Incorporated and the USDA National Institute of Food and Agriculture.
- Farmer Anthony Jones from Dinwiddie County, Virginia, has used the app and calls it a "catalyst for the future of farming" that enables "smarter, more profitable, and more sustainable agriculture."

Overall, the Agroclimate Viewer and Planner App aims to bridge the gap between agricultural research and practical, on-the-ground decision-making for farmers by providing free, user-friendly access to critical climate and crop data.

items.title: Rooted in Advocacy: California Women for Agriculture Marks 50 Years
items.description: SACRAMENTO, Calif. — In 1975, several women involved in agriculture gathered in the Coachella Valley to discuss how they could educate policymakers and consumers about the needs of California agriculture. Since those beginnings 50 years ago, California Women for Agriculture (CWA) has grown to become the most active all-volunteer agricultural organization in the state. Its […] The post Rooted in Advocacy: California Women for Agriculture Marks 50 Years appeared first on Morning Ag Cli
items.summary:
CWA was founded in 1975 by several women in the Coachella Valley to educate policymakers and consumers about California agriculture. Today, the all-volunteer organization has 1,500 members representing farmers, ranchers, bankers, lawyers, and food producers across the state.

CWA's mission is to advocate for, promote, and educate the public about California agriculture. The group has 19 local chapters that host "showcase" educational programs, such as Lake County's AgVenture program that provides in-depth training on local crops to community leaders. 

CWA's advocacy efforts focus on engaging with local, state, and federal policymakers to ensure legislation supports California's farmers and ranchers. The organization hosts an annual 2-day event in Sacramento and partners with American Agri Women to meet with Congress in Washington, D.C.

To mark the 50th anniversary, CWA recently held a celebratory "Golden Weekend" event in La Quinta, where the group was founded. At the event, the organization's first state president, Cherry Ishimatsu, celebrated her 100th birthday.

CWA has been supported for over 20 years by five Farm Credit organizations serving California - AgWest Farm Credit, American AgCredit, CoBank, Colusa-Glenn Farm Credit, and Fresno Madera Farm Credit. These institutions are part of the nationwide Farm Credit System, the largest provider of credit to U.S. agriculture.

Looking ahead, CWA plans to continue advocating to "secure our food supply, strengthen rural communities, and build our economies." The organization has also established the California Women for Agriculture Foundation to provide scholarships and leadership programs for the next generation of female agricultural leaders.

items.title: Ag Producers Can Apply for '23 & '24 Hurricane Disaster Relief
items.description: TALLAHASSEE, Fla. – Today, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture Wilton Simpson announced that Florida’s agricultural producers can now apply for more than $600 million in disaster assistance for impacts from the 2023 and 2024 hurricane seasons. Through the Florida Block Grant Disaster Relief Program, eligible agricultural producers can apply for grant funding to assist with infrastructure damage, market loss, citrus loss, and […] The post Ag Producers Can Apply for '23 & '24
items.summary:
Farmers in Florida can now apply for over $600 million in disaster assistance to help with infrastructure damage, market loss, citrus loss, and timber damage from the 2023 and 2024 hurricane seasons. 

The Florida Block Grant Disaster Relief Program is being administered by the Florida Department of Agriculture and Consumer Services (FDACS). Eligible agricultural producers in counties designated as primary or contiguous disaster areas can apply for the grants, which are funded by the federal government.

The application period opens on February 25, 2026 and all completed applications must be submitted by August 25, 2026 or until the funds are exhausted, whichever comes first. Producers are encouraged to review eligibility information and gather required documentation before starting the application process.

In addition, Florida Commissioner of Agriculture Wilton Simpson has asked the federal government for approval to use the disaster block grant program to provide relief for agricultural producers impacted by recent freezes. Preliminary estimates indicate over $3 billion in total losses across Florida's agricultural sectors due to the freezes.

The Florida Farm Bureau has also established a disaster relief fund to assist farmers and ranchers who have suffered significant losses from weather-related events and natural disasters.

items.title: USDA ready to return South Building and Braddock Place
items.description: Vacating and returning underutilized facilities to GSA is the first phase of USDA’s reorganization plan.
items.summary:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) is preparing to vacate and return the South Building and Braddock Place facilities to the General Services Administration (GSA). This is the first phase of USDA's reorganization plan. 

The South Building in Washington, D.C. has a total of 670,000 square feet, while the Braddock Place facility in Alexandria, Virginia has 160,000 square feet. USDA currently occupies both facilities but deems them underutilized.

The reorganization aims to streamline USDA's operations and reduce costs. It is part of a broader initiative to downsize the federal real estate footprint. USDA will move employees from these facilities to other locations, including its Headquarters in Washington, D.C. and Kansas City, Missouri.

By vacating the South Building and Braddock Place, USDA expects to save around $5 million annually in rent and operating costs. The agency plans to complete this first phase by the end of 2022.

This reorganization is led by USDA Deputy Secretary Jewel Bronaugh. It follows previous USDA initiatives to consolidate offices and relocate agencies like the Economic Research Service and National Institute of Food and Agriculture from Washington, D.C. to Kansas City.

items.title: USDA seeks input to strengthen ag data amid confidence concerns
items.description: The United States Department of Agriculture announced a 45-day public request for information at the Agricultural Outlook Forum. The post USDA seeks input to strengthen ag data amid confidence concerns appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
The U.S. Department of Agriculture (USDA) is seeking input from farmers and agricultural stakeholders to strengthen the integrity, transparency, and usefulness of its data products. This follows a massive revision to the U.S. corn acres, which has led to increased scrutiny over USDA data accuracy.

Key points:
- USDA agencies, including the Economic Research Service, National Agricultural Statistics Service, and Office of the Chief Economist, produce statistical reports that serve as benchmarks for the industry, such as the World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates, Crop Production Reports, and the January and July Cattle inventories.
- After the revision to U.S. corn acres, USDA leaders acknowledge there is room for improvement in ensuring farmers, ranchers, and other users better understand the processes and methodology behind these data and statistics.
- USDA is seeking input through a 45-day Request for Information (RFI) on Opportunities, Challenges, and Emerging Areas in Statistical Data, Analysis, and Research. Preliminary analysis of the feedback will be discussed at the 2026 Spring Data Users Meeting on April 22, 2026.
- USDA Chief Economist Dr. Justin Benavidez emphasized that maintaining credibility with producers is critical, as USDA's data products have long been the gold standard in market reporting.
- The agency is also exploring options for improving harvested acreage estimates, most likely without more farmer surveys.

items.title: Not the end: Testing, support could help farmers navigate PFAS
items.description: PFAS “forever chemicals” threaten farms nationwide. Testing, funding and new tech could help agriculture adapt, if the willpower is there. The post Not the end: Testing, support could help farmers navigate PFAS appeared first on Farm and Dairy.
items.summary:
PFAS are "forever chemicals" that have permeated much of the land, soil, and groundwater.

Key points:
- PFAS contamination was first discovered on a Maine farm in 2016, prompting the state to establish a $60 million PFAS Fund and testing program. Maine is now a national leader in addressing PFAS on farms.
- Experts say many farmers lack the resources to properly test for and address PFAS contamination. Without a relief and support system, finding PFAS could just end up putting farms out of business.
- In Maine, only 6 out of 111 farms with PFAS found in soil or water have gone out of business, thanks to state support. Experts say PFAS contamination "does not generally have to mean the end of the farm" with the right tools and assistance.
- PFAS contamination is often linked to the use of sewage sludge/biosolids as fertilizer, as PFAS tends to accumulate in these materials. Efforts are being made to develop technologies like gasification to destroy PFAS in biosolids.
- Lawmakers are being urged to provide financial relief and long-term support for PFAS-impacted farmers, shield them from liability, prevent further contamination, and invest in research and risk communication.

In his State of the Union address, President Donald Trump doubled down on tariffs as a key economic and geopolitical strategy. Despite a recent Supreme Court ruling that nullified much of his tariff framework, Trump claimed tariffs were behind the strong stock market performance and economic turnaround. 

Trump suggested tariffs could eventually replace the income tax system, though studies show 96% of the tariff burden was paid by U.S. buyers, not foreign exporters. 

On consumer prices, Trump claimed the cost of eggs is down 60%, while beef prices are starting to decline after a 15% increase in 2025. However, the egg market volatility may continue due to avian flu outbreaks, and beef prices are expected to rise further due to tight cattle supplies.

Overall, Trump signaled his administration will maintain a strong trade stance, even if the specifics change, as a core part of his economic agenda. This impacts farmers and ranchers navigating tight margins, high input costs, and uncertain export markets.

items.title: Strategic Farming: Let's talk cover crops!
items.summary:
Researchers at the University of Minnesota examined planting cover crops, specifically winter cereal rye and a mix of annual cover crops, in corn-soybean and continuous corn rotations.

Key findings:
- In most years, the silage corn system without cover crops had the highest nitrate concentrations in tile drainage water.
- The winter cereal rye cover crop reduced nitrate concentrations in 3 out of 4 years, while the annual cover crop mix only reduced nitrates in 1 out of 4 years.
- Continuous corn harvested for grain had lower nitrate losses than silage corn in 3 out of 4 years.
- Successful cover crop establishment and growth is crucial for reducing nitrate losses, but this can be challenging in Minnesota.

The article also discusses cover crop management:
- Cover crops may fit better in shorter-season crops like peas, sweet corn, small grains, and corn silage which allow more time for establishment and growth.
- The most consistently successful cover crop in corn-soybean rotations is winter cereal rye.
- Research on different seeding rates (30-135 lbs/acre) and termination timings (10 days before, at, or 10 days after soybean planting) found no significant differences in cover crop biomass or soybean yields.

The University of Minnesota is hosting a "Cover Crop Academy" training program for crop advisors, consultants, and ag professionals to learn about cover crop management.

items.title: After the flames: Rebuilding our ag communities from the ashes
items.description: Every year, I am struck with grief when wildfire season starts. Mostly because of the devastation and destruction wildfires cause, but also because, all too often, I have family, friends and peers who must fight for their homes and livelihood. And because I’m currently grief-stricken over the loss of homes and livestock for my friends, […] The post After the flames: Rebuilding our ag communities from the ashes appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
The fires have been 60-70% contained, but containment remains a challenge due to strong winds. The cause of the fires is still undetermined.

These wildfires have caused devastating losses for farmers and ranchers in the affected regions. One rancher in western Oklahoma lost up to 70 cow-calf pairs worth over $5,000 each. The Tallgrass Prairie region, home to much of the grazing land, has accumulated significant fire fuel over the years, contributing to the intensity of the blazes.

Climate change has lengthened fire seasons in parts of the U.S. by up to a month compared to 35 years ago. Human activity causes about 90% of wildfires, through factors like smoking, campfires, and downed power lines.

Relief efforts are underway, with the Oklahoma Cattlemen's Association and Kansas Livestock Association collecting donations of hay, fencing, clothing, and funds to support affected farmers and ranchers. Feedyards are also offering free space and yardage. 

While the physical damage from the fires will eventually be repaired, the emotional toll and loss of livestock and livelihoods will be long-lasting. Rebuilding efforts will focus on restoring pastures, fences, and herds, but the resilience of the rural agricultural community will be crucial.

items.title: Commodity farmers fret their shaky ground as Capitol Hill presses tariffs
items.description: Experienced farmers are used to tough times but for younger farmers, today’s farm economy is a uniquely challenging situation, particularly with tariffs. The post Commodity farmers fret their shaky ground as Capitol Hill presses tariffs appeared first on AGDAILY.
items.summary:
Commodity farmers are facing a challenging farm economy, with the recent trade war with China impacting soybean exports. Some key points:

- In 2018, President Trump started a trade war with China, a major buyer of U.S. soybeans. China then turned to Brazil for soybeans.

- After Trump regained the presidency, he imposed tariffs on China. However, the Supreme Court has now struck down these tariffs as illegal.

- China has recently begun purchasing U.S. soybeans again, but the global soybean supply is high due to a record crop expected in Brazil.

- This has decreased commodity prices in the U.S., leading to financial stress and bankruptcies for many farmers.

- The broader issue is how U.S. farmers can remain competitive globally, as China invests heavily in agricultural infrastructure in South America.

- Experienced farmers like April Hemmes advise younger farmers to persevere, as they have also weathered tough times in the 1980s farm crisis.

- Experts say fundamental changes are needed in how the government and industry approach agricultural systems and long-term planning.

items.title: Biologicals and the Row Crop Conundrum
items.description: Biologicals are definitely gaining momentum across many parts of the agricultural world, but row crop usage remains an issue. The post Biologicals and the Row Crop Conundrum appeared first on CropLife.
items.summary:
While biologicals are gaining traction in other agricultural sectors, their usage in row crops remains limited.

Key statistics:
- Biologicals account for only 5-10% of the total crop protection market in the U.S.
- The global biologicals market is expected to grow from $8 billion in 2020 to $17 billion by 2025, a 16% annual growth rate.
- However, row crops account for only 25-30% of the total biologicals market.

Reasons for slow adoption in row crops:
- Inconsistent product performance compared to traditional chemical pesticides
- Lack of broad-spectrum activity and limited residual control
- Challenges in scaling production and distribution
- Higher costs compared to chemical alternatives

Impacts on farmers:
- Limited options for biological pest and disease control in row crops
- Potential missed opportunities to reduce chemical inputs and improve sustainability

Recommendations:
- Continued investment in R&D to improve biologicals' efficacy and reliability
- Collaboration between industry, universities, and government to address regulatory and scaling challenges
- Education and outreach to help farmers understand the benefits and proper use of biologicals

Quotes:
"We need to keep working to improve the consistency, efficacy, and economics of biologicals to drive greater adoption in row crops," said an industry expert.

items.title: In Oregon, a Local Seafood Movement Connects Consumers to the Coast
items.description: “The fishing industry has taken a lot of hits in the last few years, and most of them hit the small guys the hardest,” says Dixon. “We’re seeing more and more families not being able to afford to maintain a small commercial fishing vessel, leading to more large businesses taking over.” Dixon, a co-founder of […] The post In Oregon, a Local Seafood Movement Connects Consumers to the Coast appeared first on Civil Eats.

The article highlights the story of fisherman Brock Dixon, who has benefited from the local seafood movement. Dixon says the movement has helped his business, allowing him to maintain his small commercial fishing vessel and continue providing high-quality seafood to local consumers.

Overall, the local seafood movement in Oregon is playing a vital role in supporting small-scale commercial fishermen and providing consumers with access to fresh, locally-sourced seafood. This trend has the potential to strengthen coastal communities and promote sustainable fishing practices.

- Hay supplies are tightening in drier areas, while other regions remain well-stocked. Round bale prices range from $75-$85 on average, with premium bales $110-$145.
- Rainfall deficits of 8 inches or more since September have severely impacted grazing and pasture recovery across central and west Texas. Some areas have received small amounts of rain, but more substantial precipitation is needed.
- The pasture mealybug, an invasive pest, is raising concerns among hay producers in South Texas if it continues to spread.
- The long-range forecast calls for above-normal temperatures and below-normal rainfall, further straining hay and grazing outlook.
- Livestock producers are heavily supplementing cattle diets with hay and feed as pasture conditions remain poor. Some have started shipping animals.
- Winter wheat is in poor to fair condition overall, with varying impacts from the dry weather depending on location. Warm-season forage production is also expected to be low.

items.summary: The EPA has repealed a 2024 rule that placed stricter limits on mercury emissions from coal-fired power plants, the primary source of mercury that accumulates in fish. Experts warn that this decision could have significant negative impacts on agricultural communities and encourage the EPA to reconsider its position and reinstate the regulations to protect public health and the environment.

items.title: The 2025 growing season in Illinois: good but not great
items.description: The 2025 growing season in Illinois delivered another storyline characterized by sharp weather contrasts, average crop condition ratings, some disease pressure in places, and very good — if not record-setting — yields in many, but not all, areas. As we have seen before, crops showed their ability to translate good mid-season conditions to good yields even with very dry late-season conditions. A tale of two springs March was 4-5 degrees warmer and 2-3 inches drier than normal statewide,…
items.summary:
The season was characterized by a warm, dry spring in the north allowing for timely planting, versus heavy rains and planting delays in the south. Crops benefited from warm, relatively dry weather in June, but moderate drought conditions developed by late June, especially in northern Illinois. Rainfall in July helped relieve the drought somewhat, but the rainfall tap largely closed off in August and September, leading to worsening drought conditions. 

Key statistics:
- Corn yield of 214 bu/acre, just below the 2024 record of 217 bu/acre
- Soybean yield of 62.5 bu/acre, 1.5 bu below 2024
- Corn production of 2.35 billion bushels across 11 million acres
- Soybean production of 639.3 million bushels across 10.23 million acres
- August yield estimates were higher (225 bu/corn, 65 bu/soybeans) than the final January 2026 estimates
- Kernel weight was the main factor reducing corn yields, with 31,400 ears/acre compared to 31,850 in 2024
- Soybean seed size was small, with 3,000-3,600 seeds/lb compared to the usual 2,100-3,500 range

The article notes that the early-season conditions, including July rainfall, set the yield potential, but the late-season drought limited the crops' ability to fully maximize that potential during grain-fill. Disease pressure from southern rust and tar spot in some areas also contributed to lower yields.

Research: Over 40 research projects are underway to address challenges like weed, disease, and pest management in sugarbeets. Breeders are also working to improve crop resilience.

items.title: American Sugarbeet Growers Association staff reflects on 50 years of policy work
items.description: The American Sugarbeet Growers Association has been working for sugarbeet growers for 50 years. At the annual meeting in January, staff reflected on the challenges and opportunities for the industry.
items.summary:
The organization's CEO and executive vice president, Luther Markwart, has been with the ASGA since 1982 and will retire at the end of 2026.

Over the past 50 years, the ASGA's focus has expanded greatly beyond its initial two issues of hand labor and sugar policy. The group now works on the farm bill, appropriations, crop insurance, disaster/emergency aid, agricultural taxes, climate regulations, political activities, pesticide litigation, biotechnology, trade negotiations, and more.

In 2026, the ASGA faced challenges due to the narrow 2-seat Republican majority in the U.S. House. Out of 12,486 measures introduced, only 68 were signed into law. This is down from 97 bills signed in the first year of the Trump administration and 69 bills in the 2019-20 Congress.

Despite the political gridlock, the ASGA achieved some policy successes in 2026, including increases to the sugar loan rate and storage payment rate, and changes to the sugar allotment reallocation timeline. However, work remains to address specialty sugar imports and sugars circumventing the sugar policy.

The ASGA continues to advocate for more economic assistance for agriculture, as the Farmer Bridge Assistance program announced in late 2025 will not cover current agricultural losses. The organization is also pushing for changes to the World Agricultural Supply and Demand Estimates to improve the accuracy of the sugar stocks-to-use ratio.

While acknowledging the challenges, the ASGA leadership expressed optimism about the organization's future, noting its effective leaders and congressional champions who can help guide the industry through the current difficulties.

items.title: Farm groups urge Trump to back down on tariffs after court decision
items.description: National farm groups reacted with relief after the Supreme Court rules against global tariffs, citing record-high supply costs. The post Farm groups urge Trump to back down on tariffs after court decision appeared first on Farm and Dairy.
items.summary:
S. Supreme Court struck down President Trump's global tariffs in a 6-3 ruling on February 20, 2026. Agricultural groups responded with cautious relief, stating the tariffs have hurt farmers already struggling with record-high supply costs. 

The American Farm Bureau Federation urged President Trump to avoid imposing any new tariffs on agricultural inputs, as this would further increase costs for farmers. The court ruled the tariffs exceeded the president's powers under the 1977 International Emergency Economic Powers Act.

Last year, Trump had claimed drug trafficking and trade deficits posed national security threats, but the court said no president has used this law to impose tariffs of this "magnitude and scope." Trump immediately announced a new 10% global tariff, which he said he'd raise to 15%, through a different law never used before.

Republican Senator Bernie Moreno called the ruling "outrageous," saying the tariffs protected jobs and manufacturing. But farm groups like the American Soybean Association urged Trump to back down, as soybean and wheat growers have suffered from high input costs and low crop prices for years due to the tariffs.

The expansion project started about three years ago, and the completion date is yet to be determined. If approved, the construction would involve more than 200 workers over two years, and the expanded dairy would employ around 40 full-time employees. It would also be an additional buyer of crops from area farms, and those farms could utilize more manure for fertilizing their crops.

The public comment period for the environmental assessment worksheet (EAW) is open until March 12, 2026. The EAW reviewed potential impacts to air, local geology, soils, groundwater, surface water, and other environmental factors. Key findings include:
- The expansion will add five covered liquid manure storage basins, increasing storage capacity from 102 million gallons to 250 million gallons.
- Pumping from an off-site well will be limited to 226 million gallons per year at a rate not to exceed 1,000 gallons per minute, subject to restrictions based on the flow conditions of the Pomme de Terre River.
- West River Dairy will construct water storage basins to store a contingency water supply in case off-site well pumping is limited during low-flow periods.
- Clean stormwater will be collected and directed into the water storage basins, avoiding contact with manure or feed storage areas.

After the public comment period, the Minnesota Pollution Control Agency will review all comments and determine whether additional environmental review will be necessary. If no further review is needed, the project will proceed through the permitting process.

items.title: How to Define Success Metrics for Your Ag Equipment GTM Campaign
items.description: Marketing campaigns rarely fail because of the creative missing the mark. They fail because they are measured against the wrong objective. Too often, performance is summarized in a single number: click-through rate. CTR is easy to report, easy to benchmark and easy to optimize toward. But easy does not mean effective. Clicks do not sell […] The post How to Define Success Metrics for Your Ag Equipment GTM Campaign appeared first on Farm Journal.
items.summary:
Key Takeaways:

- Marketing campaigns often fail because they are measured against the wrong objectives, with a common metric being click-through rate (CTR) which does not necessarily translate to equipment sales.

- OEM (Original Equipment Manufacturer) campaigns focused on brand-level marketing should measure metrics like reach, engagement, view-through conversions, and branded search lift, rather than just CTR.

- Dealer-focused campaigns should measure tangible results like phone calls, form submissions, test drive inquiries, and verified local buyer engagement, rather than just impressions or traffic.

- Optimizing for clicks can skew the audience toward high-frequency digital engagers rather than serious buyers, which is problematic in high-consideration categories like agricultural equipment.

- As farmer budgets tighten and dealer relationships face pressure, OEMs need to demonstrate brand value and support downstream sales, requiring disciplined alignment between objectives, audience strategy, and measurement framework.

- The solution is to define clear business objectives (OEM brand vs. dealer demand), select the appropriate audience strategy, and choose measurement metrics that validate attention and qualified intent, not just activity.

items.title: Is sulfur a mobile nutrient? Carryover, soybean needs, and S fertilizer product differences
items.summary:
Key Takeaways:

- Sulfur can carry over in Minnesota soils for at least 2 years after application, providing enough sulfur for corn crops. Applying 10 lbs/acre of sulfate for 4 years resulted in carryover that covered corn's sulfur needs for 2 additional years.

- Soybeans do need sulfur, but direct sulfur application may not always benefit soybean yield. Sulfur applied for the preceding corn crop is usually sufficient for the following soybean crop.

- Elemental sulfur and sulfur-bentonite products like Tiger-Sul can be slower to become available than sulfate sources. Immediate incorporation of these products can reduce availability.

- Recommended practices:
  - Apply sulfur to high-demand crops like corn, alfalfa, and canola. Soybean may not need direct sulfur application.
  - Fall application of sulfate can be effective, as it can carry over to the next spring.
  - For elemental/bentonite products, avoid immediate incorporation after application to allow for better dispersal and oxidation.
  - Consider applying additional sulfate or thiosulfate for a few years when using elemental/bentonite products, until the previous sulfur applications become fully available.

The article was funded by the Agricultural Fertilizer Research and Education Council (AFREC) and the Minnesota Soybean Research and Promotion Council.

items.title: 5 Cover Crops You Can Plant in February
items.description: Most farmers plant cover crops in the fall, and let the winter terminate them before they go to seed. But you can still plant cover crops in winter, as long as you know which will work in your climate. Plant these five cover crops this month for early spring benefits. The post 5 Cover Crops You Can Plant in February appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Spinach: Spinach is an easy cold-season ground cover that increases good soil bacteria and fungi, especially beneficial for growing peppers later. It requires soil temperatures of at least 40°F (4°C) to germinate.

2. Kale: Kale cover crops feed the soil, farmers, and livestock. It requires slightly warmer soil of at least 45°F (7°C) to grow. Resistant varieties are recommended in areas with year-round diseases.

3. Daikon radish: Also called forage radishes, these have deep taproots that break up compacted soil and scavenge leftover nitrogen. They require soil temperatures of at least 65°F (18°C) to plant.

4. Oats: Oats grow quickly, cover soil, and form beneficial relationships with fungi. Planting a mix of oats and peas provides nitrogen-fixing benefits. Oats can tolerate temperatures down to 20°F (-7°C).

5. Buckwheat: Buckwheat is a quick-maturing cover crop that conditions poor soil and attracts pollinators. It can be used as a mulch after termination.

The article recommends sowing these cover crops at rates of 4-6 oz per 100 sq ft. Using low tunnels can help provide extra warmth and protection in colder climates. Planting spring crops after these cover crops can boost subsequent yields.

items.title: Frosting Seeding Legumes
items.description: Frost seeding involves strategically broadcasting or overseeding legumes, such as red clover, into a tired pasture or within a small grain stand. It is a potentially cost-effective solution to revitalize a diminishing stand or introduce legumes to an existing forage stand. Frost seeding is usually not recommended with grass species. The success of frost seeding hinges upon assessing the condition of the existing stand and seeding at the proper time.
items.summary:
Key Takeaways:

- Frost seeding involves strategically broadcasting or overseeding legumes like red clover into existing pastures or small grain stands to revitalize the stand. It is a cost-effective solution.

- Timing is critical - frost seeding is typically done between mid-February and early March to coincide with the freeze-thaw cycle, which helps incorporate the seed into the soil.

- The condition of the existing stand is important. A thick thatch can hinder seed-to-soil contact, so it's recommended to closely hay or over-graze the area beforehand.

- Soil type matters - frost seeding is more successful on loam or clay soils with enough moisture, as the freeze-thaw cycle is less effective on sandy or very dry soils.

- Adequate spring moisture is vital for establishing a healthy, frost-seeded stand. Timing, soil condition, and moisture are key factors in the success of frost seeding.

- The article was written by Dr. Shelby Gruss, an assistant professor and forage extension specialist who joined Iowa State University in November 2023. Her research focuses on optimizing forage-based systems.

Attention time is a better indicator than click-through rate, as it shows if users stayed with the content, scrolled with purpose, and consumed multiple articles. This directly influences brand recall, message retention, and advertising effectiveness.

The AgWeb redesign provides a template for increasing farmer engagement and attention. This benefits advertisers by placing their message in focused, engaged moments rather than fleeting impressions. The article concludes that better attention leads to better outcomes for ag marketers.

items.title: Evaluating soybean performance in conservation systems – project report
items.description: You can also read the article in Portuguese and Spanish Introduction Recent dust storm events in central Illinois and across the Midwest have renewed attention on soil conservation, especially after the tragic May 2023 event near Springfield that caused an 80-vehicle pileup, eight fatalities, and dozens of injuries. These incidents highlight that soil loss is not only an agronomic issue but also a public safety and environmental concern. Reduced tillage and cover crops are well-established pract
items.summary:
Key Findings:
- Field trials were conducted in 2024-2025 across 6 sites in central Illinois and north-central Iowa to evaluate soybean performance under different tillage (conventional, strip-till, no-till) and cover crop (no cover, cereal rye) systems.
- Starter fertilizer (15 lbs N/acre, or 15 lbs N + 10 lbs S/acre) provided an early-season boost in soybean biomass and leaf greenness compared to no starter, but these differences did not persist to later growth stages.
- Soybean grain yields ranged from 60-95 bushels/acre across trials, and were not significantly affected by tillage system or starter fertilizer.
- When accounting for operational costs, no-till had the highest partial net return, followed by strip-till and conventional tillage. No-till with cereal rye had the lowest partial net return due to cover crop management costs.
- Trials will continue in 2026 to track medium-term soil, residue, and nutrient dynamics under conservation systems.

Key Numbers:
- Soybean yields: 60-95 bushels/acre
- Starter fertilizer increased V4 biomass by ~12% on average
- No-till average yield: 77.6 bu/acre
- Strip-till average yield: 78.4 bu/acre
- Conventional tillage average yield: 78.4 bu/acre
- No-till with cereal rye average yield: 76.2 bu/acre
- Starter fertilizer cost: $55/acre for cover crop management

Key Dates:
- Field trials conducted in 2024-2025
- Trials to continue in 2026

Key People/Organizations:
- Researchers: Giovani Preza Fontes, Federico Rolle, John Jones (University of Illinois)
- Funder: Illinois Soybean Association

Locations:
- Central Illinois and north-central Iowa

Context/Causes:
- Recent dust storm events in the Midwest have highlighted the need for soil conservation practices like reduced tillage and cover crops.
- These practices can pose challenges for soybean establishment and early-season growth due to cool, wet soils and immobilization of soil nitrogen.

Impacts for Farmers:
- Soybeans can maintain yields under reduced tillage and cover crop systems, though starter fertilizer may not consistently boost yields.
- No-till can provide the highest partial net returns, but cover crop costs can reduce profitability of no-till with cereal rye.
- Ongoing trials will provide insights into long-term soil and nutrient dynamics in conservation systems.

Recommendations/Action Items:
- Farmers should consider adopting reduced tillage and cover crops to improve soil conservation, while managing potential early-season challenges.
- Starter fertilizer may provide an early-season boost, but is not a guarantee of higher yields.
- Cost-share programs can help offset cover crop establishment costs.

items.title: Forest Farming: Why it Might Make Sense for Your Land
items.description: Also called agroforestry, forest farming is a great way to work within your environmental parameters and utilize the tree canopy to produce more for your farm. Especially for those who live in forested areas, this practice enhances farm output without compromising the ecosystem. The post Forest Farming: Why it Might Make Sense for Your Land appeared first on Modern Farmer.
items.summary:
Main findings:
- Forest farming, also known as multi-story cropping or agroforestry, is the practice of integrating small-scale farming with conventional forestry. This results in a self-sustaining system that works within local ecological bounds.
- The most common form involves thinning a forest to allow the best conditions for crops to grow in the understory, such as native ornamentals, fungi, fruit, timber, and forest food crops.
- Forest farming brings benefits like improved water and soil quality, carbon storage, and diversified crop options. It's suitable for farms with existing forest land or areas near riparian zones.

Key details:
- Originates in Brazil's tropical rainforests, where it is a necessity due to high biodiversity and productivity.
- Can be implemented on small farms with just a bit of forest land.
- Requires inventory of natural resources, development of a forest management plan, and alignment with local market demands.
- Regulations may apply to wild plant species, especially those under the Convention on International Trade in Endangered Species (CITES).

Impacts for farmers:
- Provides an opportunity to diversify farm products and tap into specialty crop markets.
- Improves ecological benefits like water quality, carbon sequestration, and biodiversity.
- Can be a relatively low-cost way to integrate forestry and farming.

Recommendations/action items:
- Consult local agricultural extension, state forestry agencies, and trusted market contacts to plan and implement a forest farming system.
- Carefully consider which trees and crops are best suited to your land and local conditions.
- Be proactive about marketing and selling forest-grown products through various channels.

items.title: Purdue researchers adopt interdisciplinary approach to assessing emerging tar spot disease in corn
items.description: For more than a century, tar spot fungal disease in corn kept its distance from the U.S., biding its time
items.summary:
Purdue researchers are taking an interdisciplinary approach to assess the emerging tar spot disease in corn:

- Tar spot, a fungal disease in corn, was not detected in the U.S. prior to 2015 but has since spread to 16 states and Ontario, Canada.

- Researchers led by C.D. Cruz, associate professor at Purdue, are using a mix of statistical analysis, data science, epidemiology, microbiology, AI, and computer vision to understand the dynamics of tar spot.

- Their work is funded by two USDA grants totaling nearly $1.1 million.

- Collaborators include researchers from Colombia, Mexico, Ecuador, South Korea, and the U.S.

- Previous efforts include developing a digital method to quantify tar spot in corn, which was published in 2021. Ongoing efforts are refining the model's accuracy.

- Researchers from the civil engineering department are also involved, adapting their AI and computer vision approaches to inspect and analyze crop disease.

- A current project aims to integrate drone imagery and weather data to build a model that can detect and track tar spot progress, correlating with human disease evaluations.

- The interdisciplinary nature of the project can be challenging, but it leads to better problem-solving by bringing diverse expertise to the table.

- The researchers' goal is to quantify and model tar spot severity to provide rapid and accurate information to stakeholders and address this emerging biosecurity threat.

items.title: Questions to consider prior to replanting a soybean field
items.description: Shawn P. Conley, Soybean and Small Grains Specialist, UW-Madison Early in the growing season, abiotic (freezing temperatures, hail, flooding, etc.) and biotic (slugs, deer, disease, insects, etc.) factors often reduce soybean plant stands. A soybean …
items.summary:
Key points include:

Factors that can reduce soybean plant stands early in the season include abiotic stresses (freezing temperatures, hail, flooding) and biotic stresses (slugs, deer, disease, insects).

If plant stands are reduced below 100,000 plants/acre, farmers should consider replanting. Replanting is typically recommended if stands are below 75,000 plants/acre.

Factors to consider when deciding to replant include potential yield loss, planting date, and replanting costs. Replanting later in the season can result in yield losses of 0.5-1 bu/acre per day.

Replanting costs can range from $30-$50/acre, including seed, fuel, and labor. Farmers should carefully weigh the potential yield increase from replanting versus the replanting costs.

Shawn P. Conley, Soybean and Small Grains Specialist at UW-Madison, advises farmers to carefully inspect fields and do stand counts before making a replanting decision.

items.title: Spraying 2,4-D on Soybean in 2024?

Key points:
- 2,4-D will be labeled for postemergence broadleaf weed control in Enlist E3 soybeans starting in 2024.
- Farmers need to be aware of 2,4-D use restrictions, including application timing, nozzle selection, drift management, and buffer requirements.
- Applying 2,4-D too late in the soybean growth stage can lead to crop injury. The recommended application window is from soybean emergence to the R1 (beginning bloom) stage.
- Proper nozzle selection and sprayer setup are critical to minimize off-target movement of 2,4-D. Coarse or ultra-coarse droplets are recommended.
- Buffers of at least 240 feet are required when applying 2,4-D near sensitive crops like grapes, tomatoes, and fruit trees.
- Careful planning and communication with neighbors are essential to avoid unintended crop damage from 2,4-D drift.
